1184.title: No other gods
1184.hook: first loyalty to the one God, before money, work or fame
1184.howItsDone: Christians learn this commandment in catechism, often with Luther's explanation in Lutheran churches, and some examine themselves against it before confession or communion by asking what they have put in God's place.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the same ten commandments, counted in different ways. Your line was ten words. Today, the first of them.

A bank statement, a calendar and a screen-time report. Lay them side by side and they tell a story: what got the first hour of the day, the first dollar of the paycheck, the first worry of the morning. The first commandment asks about the same thing in older words. "Thou shalt have no other gods before me." There may be no statue in the house. But money, work, fame and other people's approval all know how to ask for first place, and they ask politely.

The commandment doesn't open with a rule. It opens with a rescue. "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." First God says what God has done; then comes the word. Loyalty is an answer to a rescue. Some readers point out that before me can also be heard as before my face, in my presence: nothing else gets to stand in the room as if it were God. Jesus names one rival plainly, as day 252 heard: "No man can serve two masters... Ye cannot serve God and mammon." Mammon is wealth, money treated like a master. He doesn't say money is evil. He says it can't share the throne. You end up serving one and using the other. Martin Luther, explaining this commandment in his Large Catechism, turned it into a question: whatever your heart clings to and relies on, that is really your god. That makes the commandment a mirror. A rival god might be a career, a reputation, a child's success, a bank balance, your own competence. Good things, often. The trouble isn't that they matter. It's when they get the first hour, the deepest trust and the final word. Luther also said this first commandment is the spring the others flow from. Put God first, the reading goes, and the other loyalties fall into their places, loved better, not less.

Ask Luther's question slowly: what does my heart cling to, what do I check first in the morning, chew on last at night, trust to keep me safe? Let one honest answer surface, even a good thing, and name it plainly, noticing how much it's been asked to carry. If you pray, you can hand it back to God in the quiet.
No other gods. The first word: loyalty to the one God who rescued, with nothing else allowed to take that first place.
Your line: first things first. It was day 394's line too, and it still holds. See you tomorrow.

1185.title: No idols
1185.hook: don't make God small enough to carry
1185.howItsDone: Christians apply this commandment differently: Orthodox churches are filled with icons that believers venerate, Catholic churches use statues and paintings, and Reformed churches tend to keep worship spaces plain; preachers in each often extend it to the ideas people make of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, no other gods: nothing else in first place. Your line was first things first.

A procession is moving, and the gods are riding on pack animals. In Isaiah, the images of Bel and Nebo are loaded onto beasts and cattle: "your carriages were heavy loaden; they are a burden to the weary beast." Then he describes what people do with a god they've made. "They bear him upon the shoulder, they carry him, and set him in his place, and he standeth; from his place shall he not remove." A god you have to haul around. A god that stays exactly where you put it.

The commandment says it plainly: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image." Orthodox and Reformed Christians count it as a word of its own; Catholics and Lutherans read it as part of the first. Either way, the worry is the same. An idol is a god cut down to size. You made it, so it can't surprise you. You set it down, so it stays put. And Isaiah turns the picture over. A few verses earlier, God speaks: "even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you." Idols are carried. God carries. Churches have drawn the line on images in different places. Orthodox Christians fill their churches with icons and venerate them, with a firm line between honoring an image and worshipping it. Catholics use statues and paintings and teach, as the Orthodox do, that the honor passes to the one shown. Reformed churches have tended to keep worship plain, wary of images in worship at all. Each is taking the same warning seriously. But the commandment reaches past wood and paint. A god can be carved out of ideas, too: a God who shares all your opinions, likes exactly the people you like, never asks for anything inconvenient. That god fits in a pocket. The God of Isaiah doesn't. "To whom will ye liken me?" he asks, and a few verses later the answer comes: "I am God, and there is none like me."
screen: `A GOD THAT FITS IN A POCKET.`

segments.voice: Ask quietly: where does God always seem to agree with me, and which people do I picture God not bothering with? Let one pocket-sized picture come up and notice its edges, then set Isaiah's question beside it: to whom will ye liken me? If you pray, you can sit with that question before God, without rushing to answer.
No idols. Not making God small enough to carry, in wood or stone, or in the ideas we keep in our pockets.
Your line: god is bigger. Bigger than any picture we can carry. Go gently.

1186.title: The Name
1186.hook: don't use God's name carelessly or to justify wrong
1186.howItsDone: Christians pray "hallowed be thy name" in the Lord's Prayer, and some avoid using God's name as an exclamation; Quakers and some other Christians affirm rather than swear oaths, while other Christians take oaths in court.

segments.voice: Yesterday, no idols: a God too big to carry around. Your line was god is bigger.

Three scenes. Spilled coffee, and someone says, "Oh my God." A handshake over a deal, and someone says, "I swear to God," already planning to break it. A banner carried into a fight, with God's name stitched across it, as if God had signed up for the side. The same name, three very different uses. The commandment covers all of them: "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain." Which of the three does it worry about most?

Some readers explain the Hebrew word behind in vain as emptiness, or falsehood: lifting God's name up for nothing, or for a lie. The verse ends with a warning: "for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain." Christians have read it in more than one direction. The familiar one: don't use God's name as filler, a curse, an exclamation. The heavier one: don't use God's name to back up something false. A lying oath. A sermon that blesses a cruelty. A cause that wraps itself in God to win. On that reading, the gravest way to break this commandment isn't a word muttered in traffic. It's claiming God's backing for a wrong. Jewish tradition guards the Name with care: in Jewish practice the divine name in scripture is not pronounced aloud, and readers say Adonai, Lord, in its place. Christians who pray the Lord's Prayer start from the same instinct: "Hallowed be thy name." Hallowed means treated as holy, set apart, handled with care. And on oaths, as day 245 heard, Jesus says: "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay." If your plain word is good, you don't need to drag God in to prop it up. Some Christians, Quakers among them, take that so seriously that they decline to swear oaths at all and affirm instead. Other Christians take oaths in court and see no conflict with Jesus's words. Both are trying to keep the Name clean.

Run back over the last day or two: how often did the word God come out of your mouth, or your thumbs, without meaning anything at all? Then sit in quiet and let the name rest, unused. If you pray, you can say it once, slowly, as a prayer, and feel the weight it carries when it isn't spent; if you don't, notice how a word gains weight when it's kept.
The Name. God's name, not to be lifted up for nothing, and never used to sign off on something false.
Your line: hallowed. A plain yes or a plain no can carry the rest. That's today, done.

1187.title: Remember the sabbath
1187.hook: rest as a gift for servants and animals too (Deuteronomy 5:14)
1187.howItsDone: Christians who worship on Sunday keep it as the Lord's Day for worship and rest, while Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists keep Saturday; practice ranges from stopping all paid work to a day shaped mainly by worship and family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Name, kept holy and not spent. Your line was hallowed.

Read the sabbath commandment slowly and look at who's on the list. "Thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, nor thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thine ox, nor thine ass, nor any of thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates." The children. The servants. The stranger at the gate. The donkey. The day off isn't only for the one who owns the house. Then Deuteronomy says why: "that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou."

The sabbath word comes in Exodus 20 and again in Deuteronomy 5, and the two give different reasons. Exodus points back to creation: God made the world and rested on the seventh day, so the people rest too. Deuteronomy points back to slavery: "remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt." Israel knew what endless work with no say was like. So, the reasoning goes, don't do it to anyone else. On that reading, the sabbath isn't only private rest. It's a limit on the boss, including the boss you are. Jesus, criticized when his hungry disciples picked grain on the sabbath, answered, as day 166 heard: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Rest is a gift, not a trap. Christians keep this commandment in different ways. Churches that gather on Sunday, the day of the resurrection, may call it the Lord's Day and treat it as their day of rest and worship. Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists keep Saturday, the seventh day. Some Christians stop all paid work on their day; others mark it mainly with worship, family and a slower pace. And the commandment was first given to Israel: in Jewish practice, Shabbat runs from Friday evening to Saturday evening. Across all of them, Deuteronomy asks the same question: who gets to rest because of you, and who doesn't?
screen: `MADE FOR MAN, NOT MAN FOR IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people whose work makes your week possible, the one who cooks, drives, cleans, answers your messages, cares for your kids or your parents, and let one face come clear: someone who rarely gets a real break. Think of one thing you could take off their plate, or one message you could hold until their workday is over. If you pray, you can name them before God.
Remember the sabbath. A day of rest, given not only to you but to everyone who works for you, the stranger, and even the animals.
Your line: rest for everyone. The servant, the stranger and the donkey all made the list. See you tomorrow.

1188.title: Honor your parents
1188.hook: honor, not always obey; care for the old
1188.howItsDone: Christians teach this commandment as care for parents throughout life, especially in old age; some churches encourage visiting elderly members and parents, and catechisms extend it to respect for elders and others in authority.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sabbath: a rest that reaches the servant, the stranger and the donkey. Your line was rest for everyone.

The cross, near the end. Jesus looks down and sees his mother standing there, and beside her the disciple he loved. He speaks to her: "Woman, behold thy son!" Then to the disciple: "Behold thy mother!" And the Gospel adds one plain line: "from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home." In his last hours, in pain, Jesus is making arrangements. He's making sure his mother will have a roof and someone to look after her.

The commandment reads: "Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee." Notice the verb. Honor, not obey. Paul does tell children to obey their parents, but the commandment itself speaks to grown adults too, the ones whose parents are getting older and frailer. Some readers hear in the Hebrew word for honor a sense of weight: give your parents weight. Take them seriously. That isn't the same as doing whatever they say. A grown child can disagree, set limits, even keep a safe distance from a parent who does harm, and still refuse contempt. Jesus is sharp on the other side of it, too. In Mark's Gospel he criticizes anyone who declares money a gift dedicated to God so they no longer have to support their own father and mother. Religion is no excuse for leaving the old uncared for. And Paul notices that this is "the first commandment with promise": honor comes with long days attached. Some readers hear a social promise in that: a people who care for their old will last. Christians practice honor in plain ways: visits, phone calls, hard conversations about care, the patience of telling the same story twice. For those whose parents are gone, or who never had safe ones, some Christians widen it to grandparents, mentors, the elders at the end of the pew. The cross shows the heart of it: even dying, Jesus finds his mother a home.

Bring to mind a parent, or, if that's too hard or they're gone, an older person who shaped you, a grandparent, a teacher, a neighbor, and see their face as it is now, with whatever they're carrying these days. Let one small thing to say come to mind: not a fix, just weight, I thought of you. If you pray, you can hold them before God.
Honor your parents. Giving weight and care to those who raised you, especially as they grow old, even when you can't simply obey.
Your line: honor the old. Giving weight is never the same as giving in. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1189.title: Do not kill
1189.hook: Jesus deepens it to anger and contempt (Matthew 5:22)
1189.howItsDone: Christians read this commandment alongside the Sermon on the Mount, so preaching on it often turns to anger, insult and reconciliation; churches differ on war and the death penalty, with Mennonites and Quakers holding to nonviolence and others teaching just-war principles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, honor your parents: give the old their weight. Your line was honor the old.

"Thou shalt not kill." On paper it can sound like the easiest commandment on the list. Get through the day without killing anyone, and you're finished. Then Jesus sees the crowds, goes up a mountain and sits down, his disciples come to him, and he moves the line. Not just the knife. The anger. Not just the act. The word you call your brother.

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says: "Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill." Then he goes further. "But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment." He goes on to an insult, Raca, which the King James leaves untranslated, and then to "Thou fool." He isn't saying anger and murder are the same thing. He's tracing murder back to its root. Before a hand ever moves, a heart decides that someone doesn't count. Contempt is the seed: a fool, a nobody, a waste of space. That's the word that makes harm thinkable. Then he turns practical. If you're about to worship and remember that someone has something against you: "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." Repair comes before ritual. Some translations render the commandment you shall not murder, reading it as unlawful killing. Christians disagree, seriously and in good faith, about war, self-defense and the death penalty. Mennonite and Quaker traditions teach nonviolence. Other churches teach that force can sometimes be just. Jesus's reading puts all of them in front of the same test, closer to home than any battlefield: the contempt we let ourselves say.

Bring to mind someone you've quietly written off, a coworker, a relative, a driver from this morning, and notice the word you use for them in your head. Hold that word up, then try calling them what Jesus does, a brother, a sister; you don't have to like them, just set the word down. If you pray, you can pray for them, using their name instead of the word.
Do not kill. The commandment against taking life, which Jesus traces back to anger and contempt in the heart.
Your line: not even in the heart. Contempt is where it starts, so that's where it stops. See you tomorrow.

1190.title: Faithfulness
1190.hook: keep promises to your spouse and your people
1190.howItsDone: Christians make vows of faithfulness at weddings, and Ruth's words to Naomi are sometimes read at them; churches teach this commandment as faithfulness in marriage, though Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches differ on divorce and remarriage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, do not kill, traced back to contempt in the heart. Your line was not even in the heart.

On the road out of Moab, three widows stop walking. Naomi, the mother-in-law, tells her two daughters-in-law to go home. She has nothing left to give them. One, Orpah, kisses her goodbye and turns back. The other, Ruth, won't let go: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Those words aren't spoken between a husband and wife. They're spoken between two women with nothing left but each other. Today: the commandment about adultery, and the larger thing it protects.

The commandment itself is short: "Thou shalt not commit adultery." It guards marriage, the promise two people make to belong to each other. But scripture keeps setting that promise inside a bigger one: God's faithfulness to people who aren't always faithful back. The prophet Hosea is told to keep loving a wife who leaves him, as a living picture of God's love for a wandering people. Lamentations, a book of grief over a ruined city, still says: "great is thy faithfulness." And the second letter to Timothy says: "If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself." In this reading, faithfulness isn't first a rule about bodies. It's a reflection of who God is. Jesus takes this commandment inward, the way he did with killing: looking at someone with lust, he says, is already adultery in the heart. Faithfulness starts where nobody else can see. And its reach goes wider than marriage. Ruth isn't married to Naomi. She simply won't leave. Friendships, families, congregations and teams all run on kept promises. Churches differ on marriage and divorce. Catholics and Orthodox Christians understand marriage as a sacrament; the Catholic Church teaches that a valid sacramental marriage, once consummated, can't be dissolved, while Orthodox churches can allow a second marriage in some cases. Protestant churches hold a range of views. Underneath all of them, the commandment asks the same plain thing: when you've given your word, keep it.

Bring to mind a promise you're keeping halfway, I'll call more, I'll be there, I'll fix that, to a spouse, a friend, a child, a team, and hold it honestly, without excuses and without beating yourself up. What would keeping it fully look like, in one concrete act? If you pray, you can ask God for help to keep it.
Faithfulness. Keeping the promises you've made, to a spouse and to your people, the way scripture says God keeps his.
Your line: faithful. That's a week of commandments: no other gods, no idols, the Name, the sabbath, parents, killing, and now faithfulness. Same time tomorrow.
